games.title: PAT 2021: quick quiz
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 1 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 24-year-old cyclist falls onto his shoulder, forcefully widening the angle between his neck and shoulder. Physical examination reveals an upper limb hanging by the side, medially rotated, with the forearm pronated. Which root of the brachial plexus is most likely injured in this patient?
questions.explanation: An upper trunk brachial plexus injury (Erb-Duchenne palsy) primarily involves the C5 and C6 nerve roots.

questions.q: During a procedure, a clinician identifies the femoral triangle to administer a nerve block. Which structure forms the lateral boundary of the femoral triangle?
questions.explanation: The femoral triangle is bounded superiorly by the inguinal ligament, medially by the medial border of adductor longus, and laterally by the medial border of sartorius.

questions.q: A medical student is practicing cardiac auscultation. Where is the optimal landmark to listen to the aortic valve?
options: Left second intercostal space at the sternal border
Right second intercostal space at the sternal border
Left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line
Left fourth intercostal space at the sternal border
questions.explanation: The aortic valve area is best auscultated at the right second intercostal space adjacent to the sternal border.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with a painful groin swelling diagnosed as an indirect inguinal hernia. Through which anatomical structure does an indirect hernia enter the inguinal canal?
questions.explanation: Indirect inguinal hernias enter the inguinal canal laterally to the inferior epigastric vessels via the deep inguinal ring.

questions.q: An obstetrician performs a pudendal nerve block prior to an episiotomy. Which bony landmark is palpated transvaginally to guide the needle to the pudendal nerve?
questions.explanation: The pudendal nerve crosses the posterior surface of the ischial spine near its attachment to the sacrospinous ligament.

questions.q: A patient suffers facial trauma resulting in loss of cutaneous sensation over the tip of the nose. Which nerve provides sensory innervation to this specific region?
options: Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1)
Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2)
Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3)
questions.explanation: The skin over the tip of the nose is innervated by the external nasal nerve, a terminal branch of the ophthalmic nerve (V1).

questions.q: A mid-shaft fracture of the humerus poses a significant risk of damage to which nerve and arterial pair running together in the radial groove?
options: Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
Ulnar nerve and superior ulnar collateral artery
questions.explanation: The radial nerve and profunda brachii artery travel together in the radial groove along the posterior mid-shaft of the humerus.

questions.q: A child accidentally swallows a small foreign object which passes into the tracheobronchial tree. Anatomically, why is the object more likely to lodge in the right main bronchus than the left?
options: The right main bronchus is longer and more horizontal
The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical
The right main bronchus branches directly off the larynx
The right main bronchus has a smaller diameter
questions.explanation: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and oriented more vertically than the left main bronchus, making aspirated items more prone to enter it.

questions.q: Which of the following vessels is a direct branch of the celiac trunk?
questions.explanation: The celiac trunk typically divides into three direct branches: the left gastric artery, the splenic artery, and the common hepatic artery.

questions.q: Through which structure does cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow to travel from the third ventricle directly into the fourth ventricle?
questions.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) connects the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle within the midbrain.

games.title: Contraception and Family Planning: quick quiz
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents requesting contraception. She has a history of migraine with aura. Which of the following contraceptive methods is classified as UKMEC 4 (unacceptable health risk)?
questions.explanation: Combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC 4 (contraindicated) in women with migraine with aura due to a significantly increased risk of ischemic stroke.

questions.q: A 24-year-old woman presents requesting emergency contraception after unprotected sexual intercourse that occurred 96 hours (4 days) ago. She has regular 28-day cycles. Which oral emergency contraceptive option is licensed for use up to 120 hours post-coitus?
questions.explanation: Ulipristal acetate is a progesterone receptor modulator licensed for emergency contraception up to 120 hours (5 days) after unprotected intercourse, whereas levonorgestrel is licensed up to 72 hours.

questions.q: Which of the following is the most effective form of emergency contraception?
questions.explanation: The copper intrauterine device is the most effective method of emergency contraception, with a failure rate of less than 0.1%.

questions.q: A 26-year-old woman using depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) injections for contraception is concerned about long-term side effects. Which of the following is a recognized effect associated with long-term DMPA use?
questions.explanation: DMPA use is associated with a small, temporary reduction in bone mineral density, which generally recovers after discontinuation.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman taking a standard monophasic combined oral contraceptive pill (30 mcg ethinylestradiol) missed 2 pills in the first week of her pack (days 1 and 2). She had unprotected sex on day 3. What is the correct management strategy?
options: Take the most recent missed pill, continue the pack, and no extra precautions or emergency contraception are needed
Take the most recent missed pill, continue the pack, use condoms for 7 days, and seek emergency contraception
Stop the current pack, wait for withdrawal bleeding, and restart a new pack
Take all missed pills at once and continue the pack normally
questions.explanation: If 2 or more pills are missed in week 1, the patient should take the most recent missed pill, use condoms for 7 days, and obtain emergency contraception if unprotected sex occurred in week 1 or the pill-free interval.

questions.q: Which mechanism represents the primary mode of action of the 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS)?
options: Endometrial atrophy and cervical mucus thickening
Induction of a toxic chemical reaction to sperm via copper ions
questions.explanation: The levonorgestrel IUS primarily acts locally by thickening cervical mucus to block sperm passage and suppressing endometrial proliferation.

questions.q: A 28-year-old non-breastfeeding woman delivers a healthy infant. From which postpartum day is effective contraception required to prevent pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Contraception is required starting from day 21 postpartum because ovulation does not occur before day 21 after childbirth.

questions.q: Up to how many days after the calculated earliest estimated date of ovulation can a copper intrauterine device (Cu-IUD) be inserted for emergency contraception?
questions.explanation: A Cu-IUD can be inserted up to 5 days after unprotected sexual intercourse or up to 5 days after the earliest estimated date of ovulation.

questions.q: What is the late-pill threshold window for a desogestrel-only progestogen pill (75 micrograms) before extra contraceptive precautions (e.g., condoms) are required?
questions.explanation: Desogestrel-containing progestogen-only pills have a 12-hour delayed-dose window, whereas traditional POPs (e.g., levonorgestrel, norethisterone) have a 3-hour window.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman taking carbamazepine for epilepsy requires highly effective contraception. Which of the following methods is unaffected by liver enzyme-inducing medications?
questions.explanation: Intrauterine methods like the LNG-IUS work locally in the uterus and their contraceptive efficacy is unaffected by hepatic enzyme-inducing drugs.

games.title: General pathology — Past Paper: case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 3 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with acute severe left-sided chest pain radiating to his jaw. Troponin levels are markedly elevated, and an ECG confirms an acute myocardial infarction. If tissue from the affected myocardial region were examined 3 days post-event, which type of necrosis would predominate?
questions.explanation: Myocardial infarction typically results in coagulative necrosis due to sudden ischemia, which preserves the basic cell outline for several days.

questions.q: A 34-year-old female presents with chronic cough, night sweats, and weight loss. A lung biopsy reveals necrotizing granulomas with central acellular debris surrounded by epithelioid histiocytes and Langhans giant cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Caseating (necrotizing) granulomatous inflammation with Langhans giant cells is characteristically caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with a raised, hyperpigmented, itchy scar over his sternum that developed 6 months after a minor burn. Physical examination reveals that the lesion extends significantly beyond the original boundaries of the wound. Which of the following best describes this lesion?
questions.explanation: Keloids characteristically extend beyond the margins of the original wound due to excessive collagen synthesis and do not spontaneously regress.

questions.q: A 48-year-old male long-term smoker undergoes an endobronchial biopsy during workup for a chronic cough. Microscopic examination of the bronchial mucosa demonstrates replacement of normal pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium by stratified squamous epithelium. Which cellular adaptation is demonstrated in this biopsy?
questions.explanation: Squamous metaplasia is the reversible conversion of one differentiated adult cell type (columnar) to another (squamous) in response to chronic irritation.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male suffers a comminuted fracture of the right femur in a motor vehicle accident. Forty-eight hours later, he develops sudden dyspnea, confusion, and a petechial rash over his chest and neck. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The classic triad of fat embolism syndrome—hypoxemia, neurological impairment, and petechial rash—typically occurs 24 to 72 hours after major long-bone fractures.

questions.q: A 62-year-old female with a 15-year history of severe rheumatoid arthritis develops nephrotic-range proteinuria and progressive renal failure. A renal biopsy demonstrates extracellular amorphous eosinophilic deposits that exhibit apple-green birefringence under polarized light with Congo red stain. What is the most likely underlying condition?
questions.explanation: Secondary (AA) amyloidosis arises from chronic systemic inflammation such as rheumatoid arthritis, with Congo red stain demonstrating characteristic apple-green birefringence under polarized light.

questions.q: A 45-year-old female presents with severe abdominal pain and flushing 15 minutes after a bee sting. On examination, she is hypotensive and tachycardic with generalized urticaria and diffuse respiratory wheezing. Which hypersensitivity mechanism is responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis triggered by insect stings is a Type I IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity reaction caused by mast cell degranulation.

questions.q: A research study examines tumor cells undergoing apoptosis in response to chemotherapy. Analysis shows mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization resulting in the leakage of cytochrome c into the cytosol. Which initiator caspase is directly activated as part of this pathway?
questions.explanation: In the intrinsic apoptotic pathway, cytosolic cytochrome c binds Apaf-1 to form the apoptosome, which directly recruits and activates initiator Caspase-9.

games.title: Protein Energy Malnutrition: case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 14-month-old boy is brought to the clinic due to poor weight gain and chronic diarrhea. Physical examination reveals severe muscle wasting, loss of subcutaneous fat resulting in an old-man appearance ("monkey facies"), and a weight-for-height Z-score of <-3 SD, but no peripheral edema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Marasmus is characterized by severe wasting of muscle and subcutaneous fat tissue without generalized edema, typically resulting from severe energy deficiency.

questions.q: An 18-month-old girl presents with lethargy, poor appetite, and progressive swelling over the last three weeks. On examination, she has generalized pitting edema, hair discoloration ("flag sign"), hyperpigmented skin lesions that resemble flaky paint, and hepatomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Kwashiorkor presents with generalized edema, dermatosis, hair changes, and hepatomegaly, resulting primarily from severe protein deficiency despite adequate or variable caloric intake.

questions.q: A 2-year-old boy with severe acute malnutrition is admitted to the pediatric ward with lethargy and hypothermia (rectal temperature 35.1°C). Bedside testing shows a blood glucose level of 2.2 mmol/L. What is the immediate next best step in management?
options: Give 10% dextrose solution orally or IV and rewarm the child
Infuse a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus over 10 minutes
questions.explanation: Hypoglycemia and hypothermia often coexist in severe acute malnutrition and require immediate treatment with 10% dextrose solution alongside gentle rewarming.

questions.q: A 15-month-old female with marasmic kwashiorkor requires rehydration for mild-to-moderate dehydration secondary to acute watery gastroenteritis. She shows signs of dehydration but has no features of septic shock. Which fluid regimen is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: ReSoMal is specifically formulated for malnourished children because standard ORS contains excess sodium, which can precipitate heart failure in severe acute malnutrition.

questions.q: A 20-month-old boy with severe acute malnutrition is admitted to the hospital and started on the stabilization phase of management using F-75 formula. Which of the following routine micronutrient interventions should be EXCLUDED during this initial stabilization phase?
questions.explanation: Iron supplementation must be withheld during the initial stabilization phase because free iron can exacerbate oxidative stress and enhance bacterial growth during active infection.

questions.q: A 3-year-old girl with severe marasmus is started on rapid high-calorie enteral feeds. Forty-eight hours after initiating feeds, she develops generalized weakness, confusion, tachycardia, and respiratory distress. Which electrolyte abnormality is primarily responsible for her presentation?
questions.explanation: Refeeding syndrome occurs when carbohydrate reintroduction triggers insulin release, driving phosphate into cells and causing severe hypophosphatemia.

questions.q: A 13-month-old infant with severe acute malnutrition has completed 5 days of stabilization treatment. His appetite has recovered, facial and pedal edema have resolved, and he is alert and active. What is the next best step in dietary management?
options: Transition from F-75 to F-100 formula or RUTF
Discharge home on standard cow's milk immediately
Continue F-75 formula for an additional 4 weeks
questions.explanation: Once appetite returns and edema resolves, children progress from the stabilization phase (F-75) to the rehabilitation phase using F-100 or ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF).

questions.q: A 16-month-old child with severe acute malnutrition is admitted for inpatient management. He appears lethargic but has a normal body temperature, clear chest, and no localized signs of infection. What is the most appropriate strategy regarding antibiotic coverage?
options: Withhold antibiotics unless blood cultures return positive
Start high-dose IV vancomycin and meropenem
questions.explanation: Routine empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment is recommended for all admitted children with severe acute malnutrition because clinical signs of infection are frequently masked.

games.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease: drug duel
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child with severe gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) unresponsive to conservative measures is prescribed omeprazole. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
options: Irreversible inhibition of the H+/K+-ATPase enzyme system in gastric parietal cells
Competitive antagonism of histamine H2 receptors on parietal cells
Neutralisation of gastric acid by reacting directly with hydrochloric acid
Stimulation of gastric motility by activating serotonin 5-HT4 receptors
questions.explanation: Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor that works by irreversibly inhibiting the H+/K+-ATPase pump in gastric parietal cells.

questions.q: An 8-month-old infant with GERD shows an initial positive response to famotidine, but the therapeutic response diminishes significantly after 2 weeks of continuous therapy. Which pharmacological concept best explains this reduction in efficacy?
questions.explanation: Histamine H2 receptor antagonists like famotidine are known to cause tachyphylaxis, or rapid tolerance, limiting their long-term efficacy.

questions.q: Sodium alginate (Infant Gaviscon) is prescribed for a 5-month-old infant with frequent regurgitation. How does this medication primarily function to manage reflux?
options: Directly suppresses baseline nocturnal acid secretion by blocking parietal cell receptors
Forms a viscous gel layer floating on top of gastric contents to physically impede reflux
Accelerates gastric emptying by acting as a peripheral dopamine receptor antagonist
Binds to mucosal proteins to form a protective barrier over eroded lower oesophageal mucosa
questions.explanation: Sodium alginate reacts with gastric acid to form a viscous raft that floats on gastric contents, physically preventing gastroesophageal reflux.

questions.q: Infant Gaviscon (sodium alginate with magnesium alginate) must be used with extreme caution or avoided in dehydrated infants or those with renal impairment primarily due to the risk of which adverse effect?
questions.explanation: Infant Gaviscon contains high levels of sodium, posing a significant risk of hypernatremia in dehydrated infants or those with impaired renal excretion.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child treated for gastroesophageal reflux with metoclopramide presents to the emergency department with an acute dystonic reaction (oculogyric crisis). Which mechanism mediates this side effect?
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide crosses the blood-brain barrier and can induce extrapyramidal side effects like acute dystonia via central D2 dopamine receptor blockade.

questions.q: Domperidone was historically used as a prokinetic agent for paediatric GERD, but its use is now strictly restricted due to concerns regarding which severe adverse effect?
options: Cardiac arrhythmias associated with QT prolongation
questions.explanation: Domperidone carries a well-established risk of serious cardiac side effects, specifically QT interval prolongation and fatal ventricular arrhythmias.

questions.q: Long-term proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy in paediatric patients with GERD is associated with an increased risk of which of the following complications?
options: Peripheral neuropathy due to vitamin C deficiency
questions.explanation: Gastric acid suppression from long-term PPI therapy reduces non-immune host defense, predisposing children to enteric infections and respiratory tract infections.

questions.q: A 10-year-old child with severe neurodisability and refractory GERD is prescribed baclofen to reduce reflux episodes. What is the mechanism of action of baclofen in this context?
options: GABA-B receptor agonist that reduces transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations
GABA-A receptor agonist that speeds up gastric emptying time
Motilin receptor agonist that increases lower oesophageal sphincter basal tone
Direct proton pump inhibitor that reduces nocturnal acid secretion
questions.explanation: Baclofen is a selective GABA-B receptor agonist that reduces gastroesophageal reflux by inhibiting transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations (TLESRs).

games.title: Mastering Joint Pathology: Arthritis, OA & Joint Anatomy: drug duel
games.topic: Mastering Joint Pathology: Arthritis, OA & Joint Anatomy
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 3 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which of the following agents is a biologic DMARD that specifically inhibits interleukin-6 (IL-6) receptors and is used in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis?
questions.explanation: Tocilizumab is a monoclonal antibody that targets the IL-6 receptor, reducing inflammation in rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of methotrexate when used as a first-line DMARD in rheumatoid arthritis?
questions.explanation: Methotrexate acts primarily as a competitive inhibitor of dihydrofolate reductase, leading to decreased synthesis of thymidylate and purines.

questions.q: Which medication used for acute gouty arthritis acts by binding to intracellular tubulin, thereby inhibiting neutrophil motility and migration?
questions.explanation: Colchicine disrupts microtubule polymerization by binding tubulin, inhibiting neutrophil activation and migration into the affected joint.

questions.q: Long-term high-dose therapy with which of the following non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) is associated with the highest relative risk of selective COX-2 cardiovascular events?
questions.explanation: Diclofenac exhibits a cardiovascular risk profile similar to selective COX-2 inhibitors (coxibs), showing a higher thrombotic risk compared to naproxen.

questions.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of allopurinol in the chronic management of gout?
options: Increased renal excretion of uric acid
Urate oxidase activity converting uric acid to allantoin
Inhibition of urate reabsorption in the proximal tubule
questions.explanation: Allopurinol and its metabolite oxypurinol inhibit xanthine oxidase, thereby decreasing the metabolic production of uric acid.

questions.q: Which of the following biologic DMARDs is a fusion protein consisting of the extracellular domain of CTLA-4 linked to the Fc portion of human IgG, inhibiting T-cell activation?
questions.explanation: Abatacept is a selective co-stimulation modulator that binds to CD80 and CD86 on antigen-presenting cells, preventing CD28-mediated T-cell activation.

questions.q: Which characteristic adverse effect is strongly associated with the long-term systemic use of glucocorticoids in the management of inflammatory arthritides?
questions.explanation: Glucocorticoids frequently cause secondary osteoporosis by decreasing bone formation and increasing bone resorption.

questions.q: What is the mechanism of action of febuxostat, a medication used to lower serum uric acid levels in chronic gout?
options: Non-purine selective inhibitor of xanthine oxidase
questions.explanation: Febuxostat is a potent, non-purine selective inhibitor of xanthine oxidase used to manage hyperuricemia in gout.
